import fitz
from PIL import Image,ImageDraw,ImageFont
pdfs=[('/mnt/data/agent_figures_C_Dossier.pdf','Original with stick figures'),('/mnt/data/agent_figures_C_Dossier_v2.pdf','Updated illustrations')]

 path=f'/mnt/data/audit_runtime/diag/montage_{idx}.png';canvas.save(path)
 print(path)

You're right to flag all three issues. The quality problem is broader than the three illustrations we just changed.

I've started a file-level comparison of the original Dossier deck, the updated deck, and their PDF exports.

**One important finding:** The supplied PDFs reproduce their corresponding PowerPoint files exactly when I render them through LibreOffice. All eight pages match pixel-for-pixel in that environment.

That means there are two separate problems to investigate:

- **Design defects:** Some illustrations are inconsistent, badly positioned, or difficult to understand. Those defects exist in the PDF itself.
- **Compatibility defects:** If PowerPoint or Google Slides displays something different from the PDF, that is a rendering or import problem that our LibreOffice export did not catch.

The PDF looking better does not mean the underlying deck is correctly built.

## The comparison confirms five specific problems

| Slide | What is wrong |
|---|---|
| **1–3** | The original illustrations use a consistent visual language: square-headed agent, round-headed human. |
| **4 — Caution** | The human figure has disappeared. The caution triangle sits over unrelated rectangles and doesn't match the original drawing style. |
| **5 — Escape** | The supposed rogue agent now has a round head, making it look like the human character. The locked box crowds the headline, and the figure doesn't clearly appear to be escaping. |
| **6 — Pipeline** | The maze is difficult to follow, the stick figure overlaps the route, and three elements forming the **X extend beyond the slide boundary**. The original checker illustration has also disappeared. |
| **7–8** | These retain the older illustration style, making the changes on slides 4–6 look like they came from a different presentation. |

## I also found why some PPTX and PDF versions don't match

<box gap={2}>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    **Google Drive Dossier**
    <badge color="warning">Older version</badge>
  </row>
  <text color="secondary" size="sm">146,911 bytes · Last modified at 16:06</text>
  The file in your Google Drive is an earlier presentation, from before the latest stick-figure changes. It is **not the source of the latest PDF preview**.
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  **Latest local PowerPoint and PDF**
  <text color="secondary" size="sm">43,755-byte PPTX · Eight pages</text>
  These match when rendered through LibreOffice, but I haven't verified visual fidelity in Microsoft PowerPoint or Google Slides. The deck uses fonts such as Georgia, Aptos, and Consolas, which may be substituted in other viewers.
</box>

There's a further issue: the original editorial presentation was substantially rebuilt when the first stick figures were added. The text positions changed, not just the illustrations. That's why comparing the earliest editorial PDF to the current PowerPoint shows broader layout differences.

## What must happen before another version is acceptable

The next version needs a **single authoritative PPTX**, with all eight slides using one consistent figure design and no objects extending beyond the canvas. Its PDF must be exported from that exact file, and the Google Drive copy must be updated from the same source.

I'd preserve the original agent/human distinction and repair the three new illustrations rather than redesigning everything again.

**No files have been modified during this audit.** The current versions should not be treated as publication-ready yet.
